system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2134-12-09 20:40:00 to 2134-12-10 14:58:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for management following a procedure to address recurrent airway stenosis. He underwent microlaryngoscopy with balloon dilation and bronchial dilation due to severe stenosis in the left mainstem bronchus and bronchus intermedius, complications of his underlying connective tissue disorder with polychondritis. Post-procedure, he was stabilized on supplemental humidified oxygen and started on a short-term prednisone taper (60 mg for two days, then step-down) and Bactrim for infection prophylaxis. His white blood cell count rose to 19.2, attributed to steroid use or procedural inflammation, with no signs of infection. He remained in no acute distress, with stable vital signs and a clear chest X-ray. He was discharged home with follow-up arranged in rheumatology, ENT, and pulmonology, and instructions to continue trach care with humidification and medication tapering.
problems: Other disorders of bone and cartilage
Other diseases of trachea and bronchus

___:
The patient was brought to the OR and placed supine. Ventilation 
was established throught existing trach and adequate anesthesia 
was obtained. The airways were inspected through the trach. 
There was diffuse severe airway stenosis in the trachea and 
bilateral mainstem. Bronchial washings were sent for 
microbiologic studies. Submucosal steroid was injected in the 
LMSB then balloon dilated to 10mm. Topical epinephrine and cold

secretions were cleared and the bronchoscope was removed. The 
patient was spontaneously breathing at the end of the case then 
was transported to the PACU in stable condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You’re here because you were having trouble breathing. We think it’s related to your airway narrowing from your connective tissue disease. The team is going to do a procedure tomorrow to place a stent in your left main bronchus to help keep it open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’ve had this before. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a common next step for you. We’ll go in through your trach, so no new incisions. There’s a small risk of blood pressure changes during the procedure, but we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time… I was on oxygen after. Will that happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, at least for a short time. After the stent, you might need a little oxygen while you recover. It’s usually temporary. We’ll wean you off as soon as you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the coughing up blood? I’ve been seeing a little pink in my secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected after the procedure. They’ll use a balloon and place a stent, which can cause minor irritation. We’ll watch it, but it should settle down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The procedure went well. You now have a covered stent in your left main bronchus. They also dilated both sides and gave you a steroid injection to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did I do? Any problems?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. There was a brief drop in blood pressure during the procedure, but it was corrected with medication. No lasting issues. Your chest X-ray afterward looks clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt feverish earlier… is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you spiked a fever to 102.8 last night. We checked blood and urine cultures. No infection was found. It’s likely a reaction to the procedure. The fever has come down, so we’re not starting antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my breathing now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re breathing on your own. Your oxygen levels are 90–93% on room air when walking. We’ll keep an eye on that. You’re no longer on supplemental oxygen, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll use a nebulizer four times a day with a Duoneb—albuterol and ipratropium. For sudden shortness of breath, use your albuterol nebulizer every two hours if needed. Keep taking your prednisone and Bactrim as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, see your rheumatologist and the interventional pulmonology team soon. We’ll send the details. You’re doing well—ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your trach care and nebulizers. Call if breathing gets worse or fever returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we sent some tissue for testing, but it was just a small bit of scar tissue. Nothing concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. But everything looks stable. We’ll keep monitoring your labs—they haven’t changed much, and your white count is still elevated, likely from your steroids or the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. No signs of infection. You’re healing as expected. We’ll discharge you in a few hours once we confirm you’re stable on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for acute respiratory failure due to severe airway stenosis from relapsing polychondritis. He underwent placement of a covered stent in the left mainstem bronchus, along with balloon dilation and steroid injection. The procedure was complicated by transient hypotension, managed with phenylephrine. Postoperatively, he required brief oxygen support and developed a procedural fever that resolved without antibiotics. He remained stable with improved breathing, was weaned off oxygen, and discharged home with new nebulizer treatments and follow-up plans in rheumatology and interventional pulmonology.
